lesson.title: Metals, Acids, and the Activity Series: Where the Bubbles Come From
lesson.summary: Acid-metal reactions are single-replacement redox reactions in which an active metal displaces hydrogen from an acid to form a salt and hydrogen gas, and whether a given metal will actually react at all depends on its position in the activity series.
lesson.body:
Acid-metal reactions follow the general single-replacement pattern: active metal plus acid yields salt plus hydrogen gas. Underneath that simple description is a genuine redox reaction, connecting directly to what you already know about oxidation and reduction. The metal, starting in its elemental form at an oxidation state of zero, loses electrons and becomes a cation as part of the salt, so it is oxidized. Those electrons do not disappear, they are picked up by H+ ions from the acid, which are reduced from an oxidation state of positive one down to zero as they combine into H2 gas. It might not look like the classic image of two elements combining, but electrons are genuinely transferred from metal atoms to hydrogen ions, which is all a redox reaction requires.

Not every metal will do this. Only metals that sit above hydrogen on the activity series are willing to give up their electrons to H+ spontaneously; a metal ranked below hydrogen on that series, such as copper, silver, or gold, will not react with a typical non-oxidizing acid like hydrochloric acid or dilute sulfuric acid, because there is no favorable direction for that electron transfer to occur. This connects directly back to the idea of a driving force from a few chapters ago: without a thermodynamically favorable direction for electrons to flow, from a more easily oxidized metal to the less easily reduced hydrogen ion, there is no meaningful reaction, and the two substances essentially just coexist.

Here is a worked example. Zinc, a metal well above hydrogen on the activity series, reacts with hydrochloric acid according to Zn(s) + 2 HCl(aq) to ZnCl2(aq) + H2(g). Suppose a student reacts 3.27 g of zinc metal with an excess of hydrochloric acid, meaning all the zinc is consumed. What volume of hydrogen gas forms at standard temperature and pressure?

Zinc's molar mass is 65.38 g/mol, so the moles of zinc available are 3.27 g divided by 65.38 g/mol, which equals 0.0500 mol. The balanced equation shows a 1 to 1 mole ratio between Zn and H2, so 0.0500 mol of H2 gas forms as well. At standard temperature and pressure, one mole of gas occupies 22.4 L, so the volume of hydrogen produced is 0.0500 mol times 22.4 L/mol, which equals 1.12 L.

The net ionic equation, Zn(s) + 2 H+(aq) to Zn2+(aq) + H2(g), leaves out the spectator chloride ion and makes the redox bookkeeping explicit: zinc goes from an oxidation state of 0 to positive 2, losing two electrons and being oxidized, while each of the two hydrogen atoms goes from positive 1 to 0, together gaining those same two electrons and being reduced. The electrons lost exactly equal the electrons gained, confirming a properly balanced redox process, and accounting for every bubble of gas you would see forming as the zinc dissolves.
